title: Drag and drop people can predict
summary: Learn when a drag should move or copy, how to show what a drop will do, and how to let people undo a wrong drop.
objective: Design a drag and drop that picks the expected move or copy, shows where content can land, and lets people recover from a wrong drop.

source.title: Drag and drop, Apple Human Interface Guidelines

hook.prompt: You drag a photo from one document into a different document. Afterwards, is the photo still in the first document?

options.text: Yes, it was copied
No, it moved to the new document
options.feedback: That's what happens when you drag within one document. Across documents, the default is different.

options.text: Only if you hold a key while dragging
options.feedback: A key can change the result, but here the original already stays put without one.

hook.explanation: It stays. Yet drag that photo to another spot in the same document and it moves. One question decides which happens.

bricks.title: Move or copy?
bricks.body: Drag and drop takes selected content from a **source** to a **destination**. A **move** leaves it only in the destination; a **copy** leaves it in both. The default: within the same **container**, it moves. Into a different container, it copies, and between apps it always copies. Holding **Option** while dragging within one container makes a copy. Changing a default? Pick what people expect and what's least likely to lose their data.

term.definition: The view that holds the content, such as a text view, a list, or one document.

bricks.prompt: In a to-do app, someone drags a task from the top of a list to the bottom of the same list. What should happen?

options.text: The task moves to the bottom
A copy appears at the bottom and the original stays at the top
options.feedback: Copying is the default between different containers. One list is one container, so the task should move, not leave a duplicate.

options.text: The app asks whether to move or copy it
options.feedback: Asking every time slows down a common action. The default here is clear, so just apply it.

bricks.hint: Are the source and the destination in the same container?
bricks.explanation: The task starts and ends in the same list, so the drag moves it. That's exactly what reordering should do.

bricks.prompt: Sort each drag by what it does by default.

items.text: A word dragged to a new spot in the same paragraph
A row dragged to a new position in the same table
A card dragged to a new spot on the same board
An image dragged from one document into another
Text dragged from Notes into a Mail message
A sentence dragged within one text view while holding Option

bricks.hint: Check where each drag starts and ends, and whether a key is held.
bricks.explanation: Same container moves. A different container or another app copies. Holding Option turns a same-container drag into a copy.

bricks.prompt: A designer suggests that dragging a photo from one document into another should move it, removing it from the first. What's the main problem?

options.text: People expect a copy, so they could lose the photo from the first document without noticing
Moving content between documents isn't allowed
options.feedback: It's allowed: the default is a guideline you can change. The catch is that this change surprises people and risks losing their data.

options.text: A move takes more steps for people than a copy
options.feedback: It's the same drag either way. The problem is the result, not the effort.

bricks.hint: What do people expect when they drop into a different container?
bricks.explanation: Between documents people expect a copy. Silently removing the original breaks that expectation and can lose their work.

bricks.title: Show what a drop will do
bricks.body: Give feedback through the whole drag. Once the content moves about three points, show a **drag image**: a translucent picture of it, so people can still see destinations underneath. Over a destination, highlight it or show an insertion point only if it can accept the content; if it can't, show nothing or a **not-allowed** symbol. Remove the cue when the content moves away. If a drop fails, animate the item back to its source.

term.definition: The translucent picture of the dragged content that follows the pointer or finger until the drop.

bricks.prompt: Someone is dragging a photo over the body of this email. Tap the feedback that shouldn't be showing.

visual.html:
To: Sam
Subject: Trip photos

Here's the view from the top!

Photo
visual.alt: An email draft with To and Subject fields and a message body. A translucent photo is over the body, which shows an insertion line; the Subject field is highlighted.

bricks.hint: Which part of the email is the photo actually over?
bricks.explanation: Only the destination under the content should show a cue. The photo is over the body, so the highlighted Subject field misleads people.

bricks.prompt: Someone is dragging a file over this list of folders. Which drag image works better?

visual.html:
Drafts
Clients
Archive
Invoice.pdf
visual.alt: A solid Invoice.pdf card covering most of a list of three folders, hiding the folder underneath.

options.feedback: The solid image hides the folders underneath, so people can't see where they're about to drop.

visual.html:
Drafts
Clients
Archive
Invoice.pdf
visual.alt: A translucent Invoice.pdf card over a list of three folders, with the folder names visible through it.

bricks.hint: Can you still read the folder names under each drag image?
bricks.explanation: The translucent image still shows what it is, and people can read the folders through it to pick the right one.

bricks.prompt: Someone drags a file over a folder that can't accept it, and hasn't let go yet. What should the folder show?

options.text: No highlight, or a not-allowed symbol
The same highlight as a folder that can accept it, then an error after the drop
options.feedback: A highlight promises the drop will work. Show that it won't before people let go, not after.

options.text: Animate the drag image back to its source right away
options.feedback: Animating back is for a drop that has failed. Mid-drag, people may still move on to a folder that accepts it.

bricks.hint: Feedback should tell people the result before they let go.
bricks.explanation: Cues appear only where a drop can succeed. No highlight, or a not-allowed symbol, tells people to keep moving.

bricks.title: Give people a way back
bricks.body: People sometimes drop content in the wrong place, so let them **undo** a drag and drop. When a drop can't be undone, ask for confirmation first: the Finder does this when someone drags a file into a write-only folder, which they can't open to take it back out. And offer **another way** to do the same thing, like menu commands to copy and move, because dragging is hard or impossible for some people.

term.definition: A folder people can put files into but can't open to see or remove them.

bricks.prompt: Which of these make drag and drop safer or easier to use for everyone?

options.text: Undo for a drop that landed in the wrong place
Menu commands that copy or move the same items
A confirmation dialog before every drop
options.feedback: Confirming every drop slows down routine moves. Save confirmation for drops that can't be undone.

options.text: Making dragging the only way to reorder items
options.feedback: Some people can't drag. Offer another way to do it, such as menu commands.

bricks.hint: Think about fixing mistakes, and about people who can't drag at all.
bricks.explanation: Undo fixes a wrong drop, and menu commands let people who can't drag do the same job.

bricks.prompt: Which of these drops should ask for confirmation first?

options.text: Dropping a file into a shared folder that people can add to but can't open
Dragging a paragraph to a new spot in the same document
options.feedback: It's a common move that Undo can reverse. A confirmation here would just get in the way.

options.text: Dragging a photo from Photos into an email
options.feedback: Between apps it's a copy, so the original stays in Photos. Nothing is lost if it lands wrong.

bricks.hint: Which drop leaves people with no way to get the item back?
bricks.explanation: Once the file is in a folder people can't open, they can't take it back out, so confirm before the drop.

challenge.situation: In your task-board app, people drag cards between columns of one board and into other apps like Mail. A tester reports: "I dropped a card on the wrong column. And when I dragged one into Mail, it vanished from the board."

options.text: Move within the board, copy into other apps, highlight a column only while the card is over it, and support Undo
options.outcome: Cards stay on the board when shared, people see the target column before they let go, and a wrong drop is one Undo away.

options.text: Make every drag a copy, so nothing ever disappears
options.outcome: Nothing vanishes, but moving a card between columns now leaves a duplicate that people must delete by hand.

options.text: Ask "Move or copy?" and then "Are you sure?" after every drop
options.outcome: Fewer mistakes, but every routine move now takes two extra taps, and people stop dragging altogether.

challenge.hint: Which drags stay in one container, and how would someone fix a wrong drop?
challenge.explanation: One board is one container, so moves fit; Mail is another app, so copy. Clear cues prevent wrong drops, and Undo fixes the rest.

takeaways: Within the same container a drag moves content; into another container or app it copies.
Show a translucent drag image, and highlight a destination only while content is over it and only if it can accept it.
Support Undo, confirm only drops that can't be undone, and offer a way to do it without dragging.
